entries.name: The Melitian Schism
entries.informalName: The Church of Melitius in Egypt
entries.region: Alexandria and Egypt (Lycopolis, the Nile valley and the eastern desert)
entries.statusWord: Added for the Library, not yet researched
entries.statusDescription: Not yet researched or tiered; added so that works in the Library have a place on the Atlas.
entries.sourcing: Rare for a schism: some of its own voice survives. A small set of its monks' letters from the 330s, in Greek and Coptic, was published by H. Idris Bell in 1924. They stand beside the hostile accounts of Athanasius, the Council of Nicaea and the church historians. After the fourth century it is known only through others' records.
entries.floorNote: At the start this was a quarrel over church order, not over belief. Later opponents said the Melitians sided with Arius's party. Those charges come only from outside.
entries.relationsSummary: A rival church to the bishops of Alexandria from about 306. It broke with them, and its members brought charges against Athanasius. The Council of Nicaea tried to settle the split in 325. Antony of the desert would hold no communion with it.
entries.why: A quarrel between two bishops in a time of persecution split the church of Egypt for more than two centuries. The Melitians kept their own bishops, priests and monks. They fought Athanasius before councils and emperors. Their letters, in Greek and Coptic, let them speak for themselves.
entries.teaser: Egypt, c. 306 to the 700s — a rival church born of a quarrel in a time of persecution, whose monks fought Athanasius and left their own letters behind.
entries.longDescription:
In the last great persecution, Melitius was bishop of Lycopolis in Upper Egypt. He began to ordain clergy in other bishops' lands. Four bishops wrote to him in protest. Peter, bishop of Alexandria, wrote that Melitius had made clergy of his own even in the prison. Peter told his people to hold no communion with him.

Why the quarrel began is disputed. Athanasius and Socrates, a church historian, say Peter deposed Melitius. The charge, they say, was that he had offered sacrifice to idols. Both wrote as his opponents. H. Idris Bell, who edited the Melitians' own letters in 1924, read it as a quarrel over the lapsed. The question, he wrote, was how long to wait before taking them back.

Melitius went on making bishops of his own. In 325 the Council of Nicaea let him keep the title of bishop but forbade him to ordain anyone. The peace did not last. Before he died, Melitius named a friend, John, as his successor, and his church stood apart again.

Under Athanasius, bishop from 328, the fight grew bitter. Socrates says his foes used Melitians to bring charges against him. In 335 a synod at Tyre voted to depose him. A man once a Melitian bishop signed the vote. Around then a Melitian monk named Callistus wrote home from Alexandria. Men on Athanasius's side, he says, came with soldiers. They beat Melitian monks and locked some up.

That letter belongs to a small set of papyri from the 330s, published in 1924. Most are letters to Apa Paieous, a priest and confessor. He led a large community of Melitian monks at Hathor, in the eastern desert. Some letters are in Coptic. They speak of prayers for one another, of care for brothers in trouble, and of bread and wheat.

The Melitians lasted long after Athanasius. In the fifth century Theodoret wrote that bodies of their monks still kept their own ways. Papyri of 512 show a Melitian priest buying a monastery near Arsinoe. The History of the Patriarchs says Patriarch Damian, from 569, drove them out of the monasteries of Wadi Habib. Bell, citing a later part of the History of the Patriarchs, puts the last report of them under Michael I, patriarch from 744 to 768.
voices: Melitius of Lycopolis — the bishop whose ordinations in other bishops' districts began the split, around 306
John Archaph — the friend Melitius named as his successor, against the terms of Nicaea
Apa Paieous — priest and confessor, head of the Melitian monks at Hathor in the 330s, to whom most of the surviving letters are addressed
Callistus — the Melitian monk whose letter from Alexandria tells how men on Athanasius's side beat and locked up his brothers
Arsenius — a former Melitian bishop said to have been murdered by Athanasius, who turned up alive and signed his deposition at Tyre in 335
entries.legacy: No church today descends from the Melitians. Their papyri give something rare: the losing side of an early church quarrel, in its own words. Most of what is known of such groups comes only from their enemies. The letters also show an organized community of Egyptian monks in the 330s, outside the main church.

documentedStories.title: A Night of Soldiers at the Camp
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A Melitian monk in Alexandria writes home. Men on Athanasius's side came with soldiers, he says. They beat four brothers and locked up five more.
documentedStories.text: Callistus wrote to 'Apa Paiéou and Patabeit, priests', at the Melitian monks' settlement. He tells them that Isaac, a Melitian bishop, came to Alexandria to dine with Heraiscus in the Camp. Men on Athanasius's side heard of it and came with soldiers. Callistus says they were drunk. Friendly soldiers hid the bishop and his brothers in the store-rooms. The others beat four brothers bloody and threw them out of the town. They seized five more at the hostel where the brothers stayed. They asked its keeper, 'For what reason did you admit the monks of the Meletian party into the hostel?' Callistus ends by asking for a few loaves, since wheat had grown dear.
documentedStories.caveat: This is one side's letter. Bell, its editor, thought its facts could hardly be doubted, but that Athanasius himself was probably not behind the soldiers' violence. The date rests on Bell's reading.

set.name: The Church of Alexandria and Miaphysite Egypt
set.informalName: From Athanasius to the Arab Conquest
set.sourcing: Rich. Athanasius and Cyril speak in their own works and letters. The acts of Ephesus in 431 and 449 and of Chalcedon survive. After 451 there are Timothy Aelurus, the letters of Severus, kept only in Syriac, and two chronicles from the other side of Chalcedon. The History of the Patriarchs is a much later Arabic work. Papyri add the texture of ordinary life.
set.floorNote: Before 451, not in question: this is the church of Nicaea's great defender. After 451, its rejection of Chalcedon's formula, not the Creed's content.
set.relationsSummary: The church of Athanasius and Cyril, and after 451 of those who refused Chalcedon. It gave Aksum its first bishop and later sent a mission to Nubia. It broke with the emperor's church over Chalcedon and kept one faith with the Syriac Orthodox. The Melitians, a rival Egyptian church, split from it, and the desert monks sheltered its patriarchs.
set.why: Athanasius and Cyril made Alexandria a great center of teaching in the Greek East. In 451 the Council of Chalcedon said Christ is known "in two natures". Most Egyptians heard that as a betrayal of Cyril and refused it. For two centuries two lines of bishops fought over the city, and both claimed Cyril.
set.teaser: Egypt, 328 to 642 — the church of Athanasius and Cyril. It said no to Chalcedon's "two natures" and kept its own line of bishops through exile and strife.
set.longDescription:
In 328 Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria. The Coptic church still counts him as its twentieth patriarch. He wrote and fought against the teaching of Arius. His foes had him deposed at Tyre in 335, and the Melitians, a rival church in Egypt, helped bring the charges.

Cyril became bishop in 412. He clashed with Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, over a name for Mary. The name was Theotokos, the one who gave birth to God. In 431 a council met at Ephesus. Cyril's side began before the bishops from Syria came. They deposed Nestorius, and he was sent into exile.

In 451 the Council of Chalcedon said Christ must be confessed "in two natures". It also deposed Dioscorus, Cyril's successor, who would not come when called three times. In Egypt, clergy, monks and people broke with the bishop the council put in his place. From then on Alexandria had two lines of bishops. One was backed by the emperors. This page follows the other, the line most Egyptians kept.

The monks of the desert stood behind this line. In 457 its people asked the monks to help choose a bishop, and they chose Timothy, once a monk in the desert. Only one bishop could be found to consecrate him, so the people brought in a second, Peter the Iberian. After 518 Severus of Antioch, driven from Syria, lived in exile among them. Over these years Coptic, the language of Egypt, took a larger place beside Greek.

Who were the true heirs of Athanasius and Cyril? That is still disputed. Chalcedon itself took Cyril's letters as a guide to the faith. The Coptic church holds that Dioscorus kept that faith in the see of Saint Mark, and that the council broke it. Both sides claim the same teachers.

Arab armies took Egypt between 640 and 642. Benjamin, the patriarch who had hidden from the emperor's men, came back to Alexandria. The conqueror told him to govern his churches again, and the church went on under Muslim rule.
voices: Athanasius of Alexandria — bishop from 328, counted by the Coptic church as its twentieth patriarch, deposed at Tyre in 335 and driven from his city more than once
Cyril of Alexandria — bishop from 412, whose letters against Nestorius both sides of Chalcedon later claimed as their own
Dioscorus of Alexandria — Cyril's successor, deposed at Chalcedon in 451 for refusing three summonses, remembered by his own church as its defender
Timothy Aelurus — chosen bishop in 457 with the counsel of the monks, exiled and restored, who argued the case against Chalcedon in writing
Severus of Antioch — the exiled Syrian patriarch who lived in Egypt after 518 and became the movement's chief theologian
Theodosius I of Alexandria — patriarch from 535, driven from his throne for refusing Chalcedon, under whom the mission to Nubia was placed
Benjamin I — the patriarch who hid from Byzantine persecution and returned to Alexandria after the conquest
John of Nikiu — the bishop whose chronicle records the events of 642 from inside the Egyptian church
set.legacy: This is one of the traditions on the map that never came to an end. The same church carried on under Muslim rule as Coptic Christianity. Its line of patriarchs runs without a break to the Coptic Orthodox pope of Alexandria today. Cyril of Alexandria is still the shared anchor of faith for the wider Oriental Orthodox family: Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian and Eritrean. The Eastern Orthodox and Catholic churches honor Athanasius and Cyril too, so the claim to their name is still shared and still argued. This church also made Coptic a language of worship, and it is still sung in Egypt's churches each week. Its desert monasteries in the Wadi Natrun still stand, and so do its painted late-antique churches in Upper Egypt. Most of them are still in use.

experienceToday.text: The Red Monastery near Sohag, Egypt — a late-antique Coptic church whose painted sanctuary has been cleaned and relit, one of the best-preserved interiors of its kind anywhere
The Hanging Church, Coptic Cairo — Saint Virgin Mary's Coptic Orthodox Church, built over a gate of the Roman fortress of Babylon and still in use

documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A Christian historian writing within a generation says the murder of a pagan philosopher by a Christian crowd brought shame on Cyril and his church.
documentedStories.text: Hypatia taught philosophy in Alexandria. Socrates, a church historian, says many came from far away to hear her. She often met the city's prefect, Orestes, who was at odds with Bishop Cyril. Rumor said she kept the two men apart. A crowd led by a church reader named Peter pulled her from her carriage. They took her to a church, stripped her and killed her with tiles. Then they burned her body. Socrates adds: 'This affair brought not the least opprobrium, not only upon Cyril, but also upon the whole Alexandrian church.' He does not say Cyril gave the order. He says the shame fell on Cyril and his church.
documentedStories.caveat: Socrates wrote within about thirty years and disliked Alexandrian violence, though not Cyril's teaching. No source proves that Cyril took part himself.

documentedStories.title: Cyril Opens the Council Before John Arrives
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: At Ephesus, the bishop of Alexandria and his party depose Nestorius while the bishops from Syria are still on the road.
documentedStories.text: The emperor called a council to Ephesus for Pentecost in 431. It was to judge between Cyril and Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople. Cyril came near Pentecost, but John of Antioch and his bishops were late. Socrates says Cyril's party met as a council and summoned Nestorius. Nestorius would not come before John arrived. They read his sermons, judged them blasphemy and deposed him. Nestorius's friends then held their own council and deposed Cyril. When John came, he blamed Cyril for the confusion. In the end Nestorius was sent into exile in the desert of Egypt, and Cyril's teaching stood.
documentedStories.caveat: Socrates, writing a few years later, is critical of both sides. The council's own acts were kept by Cyril's party, and Nestorius's own defense survives only in Syriac.

documentedStories.title: Dioscorus Will Not Come In
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Called three times to answer his accusers, the bishop of Alexandria will not come. The council deposes him for disobedience, and Egypt never accepts it.
documentedStories.text: At Chalcedon in 451 Dioscorus faced charges over the council he had led at Ephesus two years before. The council called him three times to answer. He did not come. The sentence sent to him says he was deposed on 13 October. It gives his 'disregard of the divine canons' and his 'disobedience' to the council as the reasons. In Egypt clergy, monks and people broke with the bishop put in his place. The Coptic church has kept Dioscorus as the man who held the true faith.
documentedStories.caveat: The acts of Chalcedon were kept by the winning side, and why Dioscorus stayed away is not recorded in his own words. The Coptic History of the Patriarchs is a much later compilation.

documentedStories.title: Proterius Killed in the Baptistery
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Six years after Chalcedon, the bishop the council put in Alexandria is killed in a church during a riot, and his body burned.
documentedStories.text: Proterius took Dioscorus's place after Chalcedon. Evagrius says a great riot broke out when he arrived, and the crowd burned soldiers alive in the old temple of Serapis. In 457, while the army's commander was away in Upper Egypt, the people chose Timothy Aelurus as bishop, though Proterius was still alive. Then some of them killed Proterius in the baptistery. They hung his body in a public square, dragged it through the city and burned it. Evagrius took this from a petition by the Egyptian bishops of the other side. He also reports another account that blames a soldier, not the crowd.
documentedStories.caveat: Evagrius wrote in the late sixth century and took the side of Chalcedon. The petition he quotes was written by Proterius's party. That Proterius was killed in 457 is not in dispute.

documentedStories.title: Benjamin Comes Out of Hiding
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: After years in hiding from the emperor's men, the Coptic patriarch returns to Alexandria under a letter of safety from the Arab general who has just taken it.
documentedStories.text: The History of the Patriarchs says the emperor Heraclius tried to force Egypt to accept Chalcedon. Benjamin, the patriarch, told his bishops to hide, and hid himself. The emperor's men seized his brother Mennas. They burned his sides with torches, knocked out his teeth and drowned him in a sack of sand. Then the Arabs came. The general Amr wrote that Benjamin should 'come forth secure and tranquil' and run his church. John of Nikiu says Benjamin came back in the thirteenth year after his flight. Amr received him with honor and told him to govern all his churches and his people.
documentedStories.caveat: The History of the Patriarchs is an Arabic compilation of the tenth century and later; the story of Mennas is as it tells it. John of Nikiu wrote near the time. Benjamin's flight and return are secure.

links.note:
In 457 the Alexandrians who refused Chalcedon took counsel with 'the whole order of the monks'. They chose Timothy as bishop. He was an ascetic who had once been brought from the desert to Cyril.

Centuries later the church of Egypt wrote down its History of the Patriarchs. It says the letters of Peter, its head, were kept at the Monastery of Macarius. It says Benjamin fled through the monasteries of Wadi Habib to hide in Upper Egypt.

STORIES: II.1 now carries five stories (Hypatia 415, Ephesus 431, Dioscorus 451, Proterius 457, Benjamin 644), all re-checked against vendored text and trimmed to what the texts show; details not in the vendored texts were cut (the 68-bishop protest, the bribery list, 'we shall be killed', Zachariah's blame of soldiers - Evagrius attributes that to the Life of Peter). BOUNDARY with alexandria-catechetical (Built & Live, c. 150-400): untouched. The two overlap 328-400. The school is Alexandria's tradition of teachers and Scripture reading; II.1 is the see and its people. The Library shelves Athanasius's works on the school's shelf as tradition; under the extended II.1 they belong to the church of Alexandria too. No link drawn between them in this pass: neither entry's text names a relationship to the other, and the obvious one (Theophilus against the Origenists, c. 400) is not in either text.

Bell Part III (Paphnutius) is not certainly Melitian (Bell 1924, pp. 100 ff.) and should not move on that ground.

MELITIAN SPAN: c. 306 to the 8th century (start 306, end 768). The own-voice evidence is the 330s; the long tail is outsiders (Theodoret, the 512 papyri via Bell, HP on Damian) and, for the 8th century, Bell alone. The end year 768 is the end of Michael I's patriarchate, the last report Bell cites; a coordinator may prefer end 605 (the last vendored primary, Damian) with the 8th century in the text only.

MELITIAN ERA AND STATUS: era 2 per the ruling though the split begins c. 306 (era 1 by the lines). Status Pre-Survey Candidate with the census's 'Added for the Library, not yet researched' wording: a new, untiered entry made because its own papyri are in the Library.
MELITIAN SPELLING: 'Melitius/Melitian' (Socrates, Bell's 'correct form'); Athanasius in NPNF and Bell's translation use 'Meletius/Meletian'. Quotes keep their own spelling.

The census has no entry for the Eusebian party of the 330s (homoian-arian-christianity is the later Homoian church), so the floorNote states the charge as outsiders' and no link is drawn.
